+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 54.5
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The transfer vessel was a study in minimalist efficiency, a silver needle threading the silent vacuum between Mars and the anonymous orbital station. Arthur Neegan sat strapped into a plush, contoured seat, his knuckles white where he gripped the armrests. The gentle, insistent push of acceleration was a constant reminder that he was utterly out of his element. He was a man of the rock, of dust and pressure drills and the satisfying, tangible heft of ore. This… this was weightless politics, a game played in sterile corridors and silent ships. Through the single, thick viewport, the rust-red marble of his home world receded, its familiar canyons and domes becoming mere topographic features. The corporate mining territories were invisible from here, just lines on a map. *His* plot was down there, a speck of land that had suddenly become the most valuable real estate in the system. He’d thought finding the motherlode of Azra was the hard part. He was beginning to understand it was only the beginning. The Antares insignia on the uniforms of the men who had ‘invited’ him aboard still burned in his mind. A stylized red star, Antares itself, embraced by a silver orbital ring. The Diplomatic Corp. The name was a polite fiction everyone understood. They were the negotiators, the facilitators, the smooth, gloved hand that guided the system’s business—and, it was whispered, the iron fist within that glove when persuasion failed. The ship decelerated with a soft sigh, docking with a precision that felt unnerving. The hatch hissed open, revealing a corridor of polished gunmetal grey. A man in the same severe, high-collared uniform stood waiting. He was older than the armed escorts, with a calm, patrician face and eyes that missed nothing. “Mr. Neegan,” the man said, his voice a neutral baritone. “I am Undersecretary Valerius. Please, follow me.” They moved through corridors that were more like the halls of a museum than a space station. The lighting was soft, indirect, highlighting displays of alien ceramics and star charts of long-charted sectors. It was a display of quiet, immense power, the kind that collects art while deciding the fates of worlds. Arthur, in his practical mining overalls, felt like a grubworm in a jewelry box. They entered a room that was all sweeping transparency. One entire wall was a viewport, looking out onto the star-dusted blackness. The only furniture was a circular table of some dark, polished wood—a shocking touch of organic warmth in the metallic chill—and two chairs. Seated in one was a woman. She was perhaps sixty, her silver hair drawn back in a severe bun, her features sharp and intelligent. She wore a suit of simple, elegant cut, the only adornment a small pin of the Antares star on her lapel. She did not stand. “Mr. Neegan,” she said, her voice cool, devoid of warmth but also of overt threat. It was the voice of pure calculation. “Thank you for coming. Please, sit.” Arthur remained standing for a moment, a small, futile act of defiance. “I had the distinct impression my attendance was not optional.” A ghost of a smile touched her lips. “Politeness rarely is. I am Prefect Juliana Morrigan. I oversee certain… strategic resource allocations for the Antares Concordance.” “You oversee armed men showing up at a man’s home,” Arthur countered, though he finally sat, the chair conforming to his back with a whisper. “We oversee stability, Mr. Neegan,” Morrigan corrected gently, as if explaining something to a child. “The discovery on your plot is not merely a personal windfall. It is a system-wide event. Azra is the key to everything now: faster-than-light travel, energy generation, planetary defense. The corporation that holds your lease, Martian Mineralogy, sees it as a quarterly dividend. Other corporate entities see it as a weapon to be leveraged against their rivals. The Martian Independence Front sees it as a bargaining chip for secession. You see a vein of rock.” Arthur felt a chill that had nothing to do with the station’s climate control. She had just neatly outlined the entire, terrifying political battlefield, and placed him directly at its center. “I see my land,” Arthur said, his voice tighter than he intended. “And we see the future,” Morrigan replied. She leaned forward slightly, her hands clasped on the table. “The Concordance has no interest in mining your land, Mr. Neegan. Our interest is in the responsible, secure, and unified management of Azra for the betterment of human civilization. A fractious, corporate free-for-all serves no one. It leads only to arms races, conflict, and potential extinction.” It was a grand, sweeping vision, delivered with the conviction of absolute truth. It was the ‘big picture’ Asimov’s psychohistorians might have appreciated, where individuals were statistical entities to be managed for the greater good. “The offer,” Arthur stated, wanting to shatter the lofty rhetoric. “Simple. You will sign your mineral rights over to a Concordance-administered trust. In return, you will be named Planetary Director of Azra Resource Management—a considerable title with a considerable salary. You will remain the public face of the operation, a hero of the people who ensured this miracle metal benefited all, not just a few corporate shareholders. Martian Mineralogy will be compensated fairly, and the stability of the system will be assured.” She made it sound so reasonable, so inevitable. A tidy, diplomatic solution. “And if I say no?” Arthur asked. “If I decide to stick with the devil I know?” The Prefect’s pleasant demeanor did not flicker, but the temperature in the room seemed to drop several degrees. Undersecretary Valerius, who had been standing silently by the door, took an almost imperceptible step forward. “The ‘devil you know,’ Mr. Neegan, is currently fighting a three-front corporate war over shipping lanes in the Belt,” Morrigan said, her tone now devoid of even the pretense of warmth. “They are undercapitalized, over-leveraged, and desperate. They cannot protect you. The moment your full assay becomes public—and it will—they will be acquired, dismantled, or simply buried in litigation and ‘industrial accidents’ by their rivals. You will be a casualty of that process.” She let the silence hang in the air, the implied violence of the words ‘industrial accidents’ lingering like a smell. “We are not offering you protection from a threat, Mr. Neegan. We *are* the protection. The alternative is to be a leaf in a hurricane. You are an engineer. You understand systems, stability, and control. This is the only path that offers you any of those things.” Arthur looked from her unblinking gaze to the infinite starfield behind her. He felt the immense, impersonal pressure of history, of politics, of a universe that did not care about one man and his plot of land. The Antares Concordance wasn’t offering him a choice. They were offering him a life raft, and making it very clear the ship was already sinking. He was no longer a miner who had found a lucky strike. He was a resource to be allocated. The meeting was over. The gambit had been played. Now, he had to decide how to move his piece on a board he never even knew he was playing on.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter competently executes the brief: it opens aboard the transfer vessel, delivers a dialogue-heavy meeting with an Antares official, and sketches the political landscape (corporations, Martian Independence Front, Concordance). The prose is clean and controlled, with some effective imagery ("a grubworm in a jewelry box," "a leaf in a hurricane"). Morrigan is a suitably Asimovian antagonist—rational, chilling, speaking in systems and stability. The big-picture/small-picture contrast is present, though somewhat stated rather than dramatized. Weaknesses: the piece leans heavily on exposition delivered through Morrigan's dialogue, which is efficient but borders on lecture. Arthur is a fairly passive protagonist; his defiance is limited to one line and sitting down. The ending metaphor ("move his piece on a board") is serviceable but clichéd. The Asimov reference is even made explicitly in-text ("Asimov's psychohistorians"), which is a clumsy meta-touch. Dialogue is functional but rarely surprising; Morrigan's threats are well-cadenced yet predictable in their arc. Some tell-don't-show ("It was the voice of pure calculation"). Still, it's coherent, appropriately retrofuturistic, and engaging enough. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 78.4
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The darkroom is my church, and the chemical sting of fixer is my incense. I’ve always been the high priestess here, commanding the easels, dictating the timing, my voice the only sure thing in the swirling, sanguine gloom. But tonight, the liturgy has changed. The final project paired me with Elliot. Elliot, who is all sharp angles and soft sounds, a study in beautiful contradictions. At nineteen, he’s a good six years my junior, but he carries a quiet, ancient sort of intellect that makes me feel like the novice. He’s draped in his signature thrift-shop-nu-goth uniform tonight: a threadbare band tee I don’t recognize, trousers that pool just so over scuffed platform boots. It’s a deliberate, curated masculinity that’s miles away from the performative bro-ness of the other guys in our program. I’ve been quietly cataloguing him all semester, this boy who layers silver rings over painted black nails. We work in a rhythm now, a week into these forced-proximity nights. Our silence is comfortable, punctuated by the slosh of trays and the click of the timer. I’m loading a fresh sheet of paper into the enlarger, my movements efficient, practiced. I can feel him watching me, a quiet presence by the development trays. “My whole life,” his voice is barely a whisper, yet it seems to swallow the hum of the ventilation fan, “it’s felt like I’ve been wearing a costume everyone else designed. Even the boy clothes. Especially the boy clothes.” My hands still. This is new territory. I keep my eyes on the grain of the image emerging under the light—a stark, high-contrast shot of a fractured mannequin we took together—and let him talk. My usual mode is to interrogate, to dissect, to take charge of a conversation and bend it to my will. But here, in this red-lit confessional, that feels like a violation. “I don’t know what the right fit is yet,” he continues, his voice gaining a fragile steadiness. “He feels… okay. Most days. But sometimes it’s like a word I heard in a dream. Familiar but… not quite mine.” I finally risk a glance at him. He’s staring into the chemical bath, watching our image slowly swim into existence. His profile is etched in the dim red light, all delicate lines and a determined set to his jaw. My chest aches with a feeling I can’t immediately name. It’s not pity. It’s more like… reverence. The thrill of witnessing a creation, a self, being revealed in real time. “It’s like watching a print develop,” I say, the words out before I can filter them. I cringe internally. It’s an art school cliché. But he turns to me, and his eyes aren’t laughing. They’re wide, earnest. “Yeah,” he says, a small, surprised smile touching his lips. “Exactly like that. You don’t know if it’s going to be overexposed or underexposed until it’s too late to go back.” I nod, leaning back against the cool counter. My assertiveness, my trademark take-charge attitude, has evaporated. I want to grab his hand, to tell him I’ll be his guide, to map out his identity for him with the same bold strokes I use in my art. But that’s my ego talking. That’s the part of me that’s always attracted to defined things—to masculine men and feminine women, to people who wear their identities like armour, not like a question. Elliot is all question, and it’s unnerving and intoxicating. He picks up the tongs and gently agitates the paper. A soft tune escapes him, something melancholic and wordless, a hum that vibrates in the intimate space between us. It’s a sound of pure, unselfconscious being. My attraction to him, which had been a intellectual fascination, suddenly crystallizes into something visceral and warm in my stomach. It’s complicated, layered like one of his exposures. I’m attracted to his mind, to his courage, to the gentle way his fingers handle our work. But I’m also thrown. My own desires feel suddenly simplistic, embarrassingly binary. “Do you ever feel…” he starts, then stops, shaking his head. “Never mind.” “Tell me,” I urge, but I soften the command with a tone I hardly recognize as my own. It’s an invitation, not a demand. “Do you ever feel like your own… style, your assertiveness… is a kind of performance? Something people expect from you?” The question hits a nerve so precise it’s terrifying. I, Dani, who am never unsure, feel a foundation crack. My boldness, my take-charge attitude in relationships—it’s my armour. It’s how I navigate the world without getting hurt. He’s just undoing his costume, and he’s somehow seen straight through mine. “All the time,” I admit, the confession shocking us both. The red light hides my blush but I feel the heat on my cheeks. “I think I decided a long time ago that if I was going to be looked at, I’d dictate the terms.” He looks at me then, really looks at me, and it’s like no one has ever seen me before. Not the art student, not the assertive woman, just *me*. The chemistry is no longer just intellectual. It’s a palpable thing in the chemical-thick air, a current running between the development trays and the enlarger, pulling us together. He lifts the print from the bath, holding it up. The image is perfect. The fractured mannequin is whole in its brokenness, stark and beautiful. Water drips onto the floor like seconds ticking. “It’s good,” I say, my voice husky. “We did good,” he corrects softly. We. The word hangs there. He hasn’t moved. I haven’t moved. The hum of the fan is the only sound now. The space between us feels charged, fragile, like a latent image waiting for the developer. Do I close it? Do I wait for him? My every instinct is to lead, to claim, to make my interest known with the boldness that defines me. But this isn’t my revelation to develop. So I do something entirely new. I stay perfectly still. I give him the space, the agency, to decide what happens next in the developing darkness.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece fulfills the brief with strong fidelity: first-person Dani, the darkroom confessional setting, Elliot's tentative gender questioning, Dani's internal conflict between assertiveness and giving agency, and the charged, unresolved ending. The central metaphor—identity as a photograph developing under red light—is introduced early and sustained, culminating in the closing line "this isn't my revelation to develop," which ties theme, setting, and character arc together neatly, perhaps a touch too neatly. Strengths: the imagery is cohesive and atmospheric; the dialogue is restrained and believable, with Elliot's "costume everyone else designed" line and the mutual-recognition exchange about performance landing well. Dani's voice is consistent—confident, wry, slightly self-mythologizing ("high priestess," "liturgy")—and her vulnerability when Elliot turns the question back on her is the piece's emotional high point, a genuinely earned reversal. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally strains toward the overwrought ("swirling, sanguine gloom," "a study in beautiful contradictions," "etched in the dim red light"). Some telling creeps in ("My assertiveness, my trademark take-charge attitude, has evaporated"; "The chemistry is no longer just intellectual"). The metaphor of developing prints is leaned on heavily and becomes predictable; a few beats (the perfect print, the dripping water "like seconds ticking") are familiar art-school tropes. The word count is somewhat under 1000 words, a minor adherence issue. Elliot remains somewhat idealized—soft, ancient intellect, brave—which slightly flattens him into a muse for Dani's arc rather than a full person. The ending's stillness is thematically right but borders on pat. Overall this is a polished, emotionally intelligent piece with a clear voice and a well-integrated central conceit, held back from excellence by occasional purple flourishes, some telling, and a slightly schematic neatness. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 54.8
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Roman sun was a merciless gold, baking the cobblestones and setting the Trevi Fountain’s waters ablaze. Ben, a map of the city unfolded in his hands and a guidebook propped open against the fountain’s ledge, was muttering a phonetic disaster. “*Pizza… margherita… per favore?*” he whispered to a stone triton, practicing. The roar was sudden, a visceral rip in the afternoon’s tourist hum. A vintage Vespa, the colour of blood oranges, swerved around a group of selfie-stick wielders and shot onto the pedestrianized concourse. Ben, stepping back without looking, became the immediate and unintended finish line. The scooter’s front wheel jerked, the machine fishtailed, and the rider, a woman in black denim and a helmet with a cracked visor, planted a booted foot on the ground, skidding to a halt mere inches from his shins. The scent of hot engine oil and jasmine perfume washed over him. “*Stronzo!*” she yelled, flipping up her visor. Her eyes were dark and furious. “You have a death wish? You walk backwards like a crab?” Ben’s heart hammered against his ribs. “I… I am so terribly sorry! *Mi dispiace!* I wasn’t looking—” “No, you were reading,” she snapped, cutting off his clumsy Italian. She killed the engine, the sudden silence ringing. She had a face all sharp, elegant angles, a mouth made for smirking. “A book. You trust a book more than your own eyes?” She swung a leg off the bike, her movements all efficient, contained energy. “It’s a very good guidebook,” he said weakly, then winced at his own absurdity. She leaned over, plucked the book from his limp hand, and read the cover. “*‘Roma for the Timid Traveller’*?” She let out a laugh, sharp and bright as broken glass. “*Dio mio.* No wonder. You are a timid traveller.” She tossed it back to him. It was an accusation. “Ben,” he said, flustered. “My name is Ben. And I’m not timid, I’m… researched.” “Alessandra,” she said, not offering a hand. Her gaze swept over him—the sensible shoes, the neatly buttoned shirt, the faint sheen of panic-sweat on his brow. A slow, mischievous smile spread across her face. It was a smile that promised delightful trouble. “You have apologised to me ten times in three minutes. This is a new record. I think you owe me a coffee. To calm my nerves.” Before he could form another apology or refusal, she was wheeling her Vespa towards a side alley. “Come on, Mr. Researched. I know a place. No tourists. No guidebooks.” The place was a dark, standing-room-only bar tucked behind a market square. Alessandra ordered two *caffè corretti*—espresso ‘corrected’ with a shot of grappa. Ben sipped his, the fiery liquor burning a path down his throat, and felt something in his carefully planned schedule irrevocably snap. “So, what are you in Rome for? To read about it?” she asked, leaning against the zinc counter. “I’m an academic. Medieval history. On sabbatical.” “A professor!” she crowed. “Even better. You need an un-professor day.” Her eyes glittered. “I will be your guide. The anti-guidebook.” And so it began. She dragged him from the bar, and her tour was a whirlwind of the illicit and the irreverent. She didn’t show him the Colosseum; she instead scaled a temporary construction fence nearby, pulling him up after her to point at a hidden section of ancient brickwork visible only from that precarious perch. As a security guard shouted, she laughed and jumped down, grabbing Ben’s hand and sprinting away, his heart pounding with a terror that felt suspiciously like joy. In a quiet church, while Ben admired a Caravaggio, he turned to find Alessandra not looking at the art, but deftly palming a single, long-stemmed white rose from a devotional candle display, tucking it into the inner pocket of her jacket with a swift, practised motion. She caught him staring and just winked. The final test was a tiny, hidden钥匙钥匙 keyhole in a door on the Aventine Hill. “Look,” she commanded, her voice a whisper. Ben bent down, putting his eye to the tiny aperture. The world compressed, then exploded into a perfect, breathtakingly framed view of the dome of St. Peter’s, a jewel at the end of a manicured garden path. It was magic. “How did you…?” he breathed, turning to her, awe-struck. But she was gone. He found her a few feet away, accepting two glasses of prosecco from the terrace of a private club, though they weren’t guests. She handed one to Ben. “The British are good at stealing things, no? Empires, artifacts. This is just champagne.” It was then a man emerged from the club, his expression shifting from annoyance to recognition. “Alessandra? *Ciao, bella!* Still stealing drinks?” “I prefer ‘liberating’ them, Enzo,” she shot back, though her smile tightened. Enzo, slick and grinning, turned to Ben. “And who is your friend? You have not warned him?” He clapped Ben on the shoulder. “Be careful, my friend. This one… she is a fox. Very clever, very fun. But she collects things. Experiences. People. She gets bored. It is her sport.” He laughed, as if it were a charming quirk, and wandered off. An awkward silence fell. The magic of the keyhole moment evaporated. Ben looked at her, the warning settling between them. “Is that true?” Alessandra’s defiant mask was back. “Do you feel collected, Professor?” The sun began to dip, casting long shadows. They stood by her Vespa back near the Tiber. The day, a chaotic, exhilarating blur, was ending. “I should…” Ben began, gesturing vaguely towards his hotel. “Yes. Your guidebook will be lonely,” she said, but the bite was gone from her words. She looked tired, for the first time all day. She pulled the slightly-crushed white rose from her jacket and handed it to him. “A souvenir. Stolen, obviously.” He took it. Their fingers brushed. The air hummed with everything unsaid—the attraction, the warning, the sheer unlikeliness of them. “Will I see you again?” The question was out before he could stop it, hopelessly earnest. Alessandra studied him, her head tilted. The setting sun set fire to the edges of her dark hair. She was a silhouette of beautiful trouble. She smiled, that same enigmatic, promising smirk from the fountain. “Maybe,” she said, pulling on her helmet. The cracked visor hid her eyes. “If you’re lucky.” The engine roared to life, a defiant snarl in the twilight. And then she was gone, weaving into the Roman traffic, leaving Ben standing on the cobblestones, a stolen rose in his hand and the thrilling, terrifying sense that his sabbatical had just been irrevocably derailed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent, scene-based day-in-Rome romance that hits most of the prompt's beats: the near-collision at Trevi, the culture clash, the escalating unsanctioned tour, the kleptomania shown through subtle acts (the rose, the prosecco), and an ambiguous parting. The prose is generally clean and evocative, with some strong images ("a laugh, sharp and bright as broken glass," the keyhole view of St. Peter's). The Enzo interlude is a smart structural move, providing an external warning that complicates the ending rather than letting it stay purely sweet. Flaws: the prompt's placeholder was left unfilled — the model apparently ignored it, which is a notable instruction-adherence gap (though arguably the prompt itself was malformed). More glaring is the artifact "a tiny, hidden钥匙钥匙 keyhole" — stray Chinese characters left in the final text, an obvious unedited error that breaks immersion and signals amateurish output. The word count is somewhat under 1000. Some beats are rushed (the Colosseum fence-scaling is summarized in a paragraph rather than dramatized, telling rather than showing the day's middle). Alessandra risks being a "manic pixie" archetype — the Enzo scene partially redeems this by acknowledging it diegetically, and her tiredness at the end adds nuance. Ben's transformation is modest and credible. Dialogue is serviceable, occasionally sharp ("Do you feel collected, Professor?"), occasionally flat. The ending's "Maybe. If you're lucky" is a bit stock but tonally right. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 74.8
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Last Outpost hums with its usual evening thrum, a low-grade symphony of clinking glasses, the gurgle of the synthesizer, and the low murmur of a dozen different conversations in a dozen different languages. I’m in my element, a conductor with a damp rag, keeping time by wiping the polished durasteel counter. Right now, I’m working on a particularly stubborn ring left by a miner’s grimy tumbler, circling it over and over. Zax, a hulking Borvian with a carapace that gleams under the soft glow of the overhead lights, is nursing a synth-ale and complaining about his foreman. Again. “—and I told him, if he reroutes the coolant through the secondary manifold one more time, the whole shaft’s gonna ice over. But does he listen? Does he ever listen? His cranial ridges are just for show, I swear.” “Mmm,” I murmur, not looking up from my circular mission. “Maybe he’s saving up for a bigger set. Heard they’re doing two-for-one down at the clinic on Ceres.” Zax blinks his large, liquid-black eyes, processing. Then a deep, rumbling laugh echoes from his chest. “Nets, you’re a menace.” “It’s why you keep coming back,” I say, finally granting the spot mercy and flipping the rag over my shoulder. The door to the Outpost hisses open, spilling in the faint, metallic scent of the asteroid field. A new patron. He’s tall, willowy, with skin the colour of deep space and a mess of slender, twitching tentacles tied back in what might have once been a dignified style. Now, they’re askew, like he’s been running his hands through them for hours. His clothes are well-made but rumpled, and his eyes—large, silver-coin eyes—dart around the room before settling on the empty stool at the far end of the bar. He moves with a tense, quiet urgency that screams ‘trouble’ or ‘on the run.’ Out here, it’s usually both. He slips onto the stool, his long fingers tapping a nervous rhythm on the counter. I give Zax a pat on the arm. “Hold that thought. Duty calls.” I make my way down, picking up a glass to polish, a useful prop for looking busy while listening. “What’ll it be?” His voice is softer than I expected, a low, slightly raspy whisper, like stone grinding on stone. “Vega whisky. Neat.” He pauses, his silver eyes finally focusing on me, seeing me instead of just the space around him. “Better make that a double.” I nod, turning to the backlit shelf. The good stuff. Not many order it. I pour two fingers of the amber liquid, then two more, into a heavy crystal tumbler. The soft clink of the glass on the counter seems abnormally loud. He doesn’t just sip it; he absorbs it, closing his eyes as the liquor goes down. A slight shudder runs through him, and some of the tension in his shoulders seems to dissolve. He places the glass down carefully. “Rough shift?” I ask, leaning back against the counter behind me, arms crossed. Standard bartender banter. A opening gambit. He gives a short, hollow laugh. “You could say that.” His tentacles give a collective, agitated writhe. “Mining, merchant, or running?” I ask, my tone light. It’s the usual trifecta. “A bit of the last one, I suppose.” He finally looks at me, really looks, and there’s a terrifying weariness in his gaze. “You’re Nettle, aren’t you? They said to find you.” The rag in my hand stills. The ambient noise of the bar seems to fade into a dull roar. My past is a ghost I keep locked in a very deep, very dark box. Very few people have the key, and none of them would send a frazzled stranger to my bar to use it. “Nets,” I correct him, my voice a degree cooler. “My friends call me Nets. And I don’t believe we’ve met.” “Kaelen,” he says, offering a name like it’s a peace offering. It means nothing to me. He leans forward, his voice dropping even further. “Lyssa sent me.” The name hits me like a physical blow to the sternum. *Lyssa.* The ghost doesn’t just rattle the box; it bursts out, sucking all the air from my lungs. I haven’t heard that name in five standard years. I grip the edge of the counter, my knuckles turning white. The friendly bartender persona shatters and falls away. “Is she here?” The question is out before I can stop it, sharp and desperate. “No. No, she’s… she’s in trouble, Nettle. Deep trouble.” He runs a hand through his dreads, making them more of a mess. “The kind of trouble you specialize in.” I feel the eyes of the bar on me. Zax has stopped pretending to not listen. Old Man Grith has paused his perpetual game of solitaire. I force myself to breathe, to pick up my rag and start wiping that same damn spot again. The motion is robotic, a cover for the panic spiraling inside me. “I don’t do that anymore,” I say, my voice tight. “I pour drinks. I listen to problems. I don’t solve them. Not those kinds.” “She doesn’t have anyone else,” Kaelen insists, his whisper turning urgent, pleading. “They’re circling her. The… the project. It went wrong. You know how she gets when she’s close to a breakthrough. She wouldn’t stop. Now they want it, and they want to bury the evidence. That means burying her.” Each word is another weight on my chest. Lyssa. Brilliant, reckless, stubborn Lyssa. Of course she wouldn’t stop. She never could. “Why come to me?” I snap, the words hissed through clenched teeth. “I’m nobody. I’m a bartender on the ass-end of nowhere.” “Because you’re *not* nobody,” he says, his silver eyes holding mine, refusing to let me look away. “She told me. She said if anything ever happened, you were the only one who was ever… resourceful enough. The only one she ever trusted.” He reaches into a inner pocket of his jacket. I flinch, half-expecting a weapon. But it’s just a small, crystalline data-sliver. He places it on the bar between us. It glows with a soft, pulsing blue light. “She said to give you this. She said you’d know what to do.” I stare at the sliver. It looks like a tiny, captured star. It looks like my past, resurrected and demanding payment. It looks like a death sentence. I don’t touch it. I just keep wiping the bar, the rough texture of the rag the only solid, real thing in a universe that has suddenly tilted on its axis. “Your whisky’s getting warm,” I finally say, my voice hollow.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece adheres well to the prompt: first person, present tense, cozy sci-fi bar setting, a frazzled tentacled stranger ordering the exact drink specified, conflict established (Nettle's past with Lyssa) and left unresolved, roughly 60% dialogue, and near the 1000-word target. The opening establishes atmosphere efficiently, and the banter with Zax gives a good baseline of Nets's normal life before disruption. Strengths: The voice is consistent — wry, guarded, observational. The pacing of the reveal is well handled, with the name "Lyssa" landing as an effective pivot. The ending line ("Your whisky's getting warm") is a strong choice, deflecting emotion through bartender reflexes rather than melodrama. The data-sliver as a physical embodiment of the past is a nice concrete device. Weaknesses: The prose leans on familiar genre furniture — "hits me like a physical blow," "knuckles turning white," "the universe tilted on its axis," "ass-end of nowhere." These are stock phrases that flatten otherwise good moments. There are small grammatical slips ("A opening gambit," "a inner pocket") that read as unpolished. The stranger's exposition ("They're circling her... they want to bury the evidence") is efficient but generic — the "secret project gone wrong" is a well-worn plot. Some telling creeps in ("screams 'trouble' or 'on the run'") though it's partially earned by the bartender's professional eye. Zax and Grith are thin, functional background figures. Emotionally, the piece works but stays within expected registers; the panic is described more than deeply felt. Overall this is a solid, professional genre chapter that does its job without transcending it. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 70.0
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The strap on my backpack keeps slipping off my shoulder. It’s the third time on this block. Each time, I heave it back up with a grunt, the worn canvas rubbing a raw spot on my collarbone. It’s a stupid, mundane annoyance, but right now, it feels like the universe is personally invested in making everything, even this, difficult for me. Two states. Two states between me and the shattered dinner plates, the slammed door, my father’s voice cracking on the word “*abomination*.” The word hangs in the humid New Orleans air like a ghost I can’t shake. I left to escape the feeling of my skin being a prison, only to have my own family try and slam the door on the person trying to get out. *Okay, Taylor. Breathe. You’re here. Now what?* “Now what” is a crumbling sidewalk on a street that smells like jasmine, fried food, and something unidentifiably dank. The air is so thick I can feel it on my teeth. It’s nothing like Tennessee. It’s louder, brighter, messier. A woman with gold teeth laughs a sound like gravel tumbling, and two men argue passionately over a game of chess, their board balanced on a milk crate. It feels like life, raw and buzzing, and I’m just a ghost drifting through it. My stomach growls, a sharp, hollow ache. The fifty-three dollars in my pocket feels like a million and also like nothing at all. I need to make it last. I find a corner store that’s all flickering fluorescent lights and bulletproof glass. The clerk eyes me, a tired-looking guy with a tattoo of a fleur-de-lis on his neck. I buy the cheapest bottle of water and a granola bar, my voice a timid squeak when I thank him. *Real confident, Taylor. They’ll never see you as a real guy with a voice like that.* The thought is a familiar, bitter pill. I’m sitting on a low wall, trying to make the granola bar last, when I see him. Or her. It’s hard to tell, and the not-knowing is a weird, magnetic pull. They’re leaning against a brick wall, all sharp angles and shadows, maybe a year or two older than me. Their hair is shaved on one side, long and purple on the other, falling over a gaunt face. They’re wearing a ripped denim vest over a faded band shirt, and their eyes are doing the same scan of the street that mine were, but theirs is sharper, more calculating. A runaway’s eyes. I know the look. They catch me staring and hold my gaze, unblinking. I quickly look down at my shoes, heat flooding my cheeks. “You look lost, cher.” The voice is raspy, androgynous, with the faintest hint of a drawl that’s different from the one back home. I look up. They’ve pushed off the wall and are standing a few feet away, not smiling. “I’m not lost,” I say, too quickly. My voice does that stupid thing again. A slow, lopsided smirk spreads across their face. “Everyone down here is either lost, found, or running. Which one are you?” My heart is a frantic drum against my ribs. *Danger, Taylor. Stranger danger. But what’s more dangerous? This person, or sleeping on a park bench tonight?* The memory of my father’s twisted, furious face flashes behind my eyes. “Running,” I admit, the word tasting like a secret. “Join the club.” They take a step closer. “Name’s Silas. You got a name? Or you just ‘Running’?” I hesitate. Taylor feels like a relic from that other life, the one crumbling to dust 400 miles behind me. But the name I’d chosen for myself, the one that got me thrown out… that feels too new, too fragile to offer up to this sharp, smirking stranger. “Ty,” I say. It’s a compromise. A piece of the whole. “Ty,” they repeat, and it sounds different in their mouth. Less like a lie. “You look like you could use a place to crash that ain’t a doorway. Got a spot. It ain’t the Ritz, but the roof don’t leak. Mostly.” This is it. The moment. The stupid decision that gets me on a true crime podcast. *I should say no. I should walk away.* But the strap on my backpack slips again, the weight of everything I own suddenly unbearable. I’m so tired. And Silas is looking at me, and for the first time in 48 hours, it doesn’t feel like a judgment. It just *is*. “Why?” I ask, the suspicion my mother beat into me finally surfacing. Silas’s smirk falters for a microsecond. Something vulnerable flashes in their dark eyes. “Let’s just say I’ve been ‘Running’ for a lot longer than you. Sometimes you gotta throw a line to the next person drowning. You comin’ or what?” They turn and start walking without waiting for an answer. A definitive act. A test. I sit there for one second, two, the war inside me a screaming match. *This is how you disappear. This is how you survive.* I stand up, hitch the stupid strap back onto my raw shoulder, and follow the purple hair into the gathering dusk. The city seems to pulse around me, a living, breathing thing full of dangers and possibilities. I have no idea what I’m doing. I have no idea who Silas is. But for the first time since I got on that truck, I’m moving toward something, not just away. And right now, that has to be enough.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece adheres well to the prompt: first person, mixed tense, Taylor's voice, internal monologue, a runaway encounter in New Orleans, roughly the requested length. The prose is competent and readable, with a consistent, appropriately anxious teen voice. The backpack strap motif works as a grounding device, and the sensory introduction to New Orleans (jasmine, fried food, "unidentifiably dank") is effective without being excessive. The internal monologue captures conflicting impulses — suspicion versus exhaustion, self-doubt about voice and passing — with reasonable authenticity. Weaknesses: the story leans on familiar runaway-fiction beats. Silas is a stock "sharp-eyed street kid with a hidden soft side" archetype, and their dialogue ("Everyone down here is either lost, found, or running") is polished to the point of feeling written rather than spoken. The "true crime podcast" line is a well-worn internet-era quip. The ending's turn — Taylor deciding to follow Silas — is earned only lightly; the piece gestures at the calculation but resolves it quickly and somewhat conveniently. Taylor's dysphoria and family trauma are conveyed mostly through summary ("shattered dinner plates," "abomination") rather than dramatized memory, which flattens the emotional stakes somewhat. There's mild telling ("It feels like life, raw and buzzing") and a few over-neat thematic statements ("moving toward something, not just away") that tie the bow too tightly. Still, the piece is coherent, never meandering, avoids purple prose, and sustains engagement. It's solid, professional YA writing that stops short of distinction due to conventional plotting and archetypal characterization. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The sun, a bleary and indifferent eye, peered over the rubble that was once, according to a faded and perforated sign, a ‘Bespoke Artisanal Shopping Experience’. Midas poked at last night’s embers with a stick, producing a sigh of grey ash. “Right,” he said, to no one in particular, and then specifically to his companion. “Objective for today: the old ‘Everything Must Go!’ megastore. Intel suggests a cache of tinned peaches may have survived the looting, the fires, and the general tide of human misery. High risk, high reward. Thoughts?” From his perch on a crumbling wall, Chewy the animatronic koala regarded him with glassy, unchanging eyes. One paw was permanently raised in a wave that had, centuries ago, been charming. A faint whirring sound emanated from within his matted faux-fur chest, and he emitted a voice that was both cheerful and utterly devoid of soul. *“Simply… un-be-*lievably*… soft,”* Chewy declared, with the gravitas of a prophet foretelling the end of days. “Thank you for that tactical assessment,” Midas said dryly. “Your input on textile plushness is, as always, invaluable in our struggle for caloric survival.” He hoisted the koala onto his backpack, securing him with a frayed strap. Chewy’s head lolled. *“Reach out and touch someone,”* he advised, his voice crackling with pre-Collapse static. “Touching people is what gets you stabbed these days, my friend,” Midas muttered, adjusting his grip on his ‘staff’—which was, in fact, a repurposed titanium golf club. “Let’s go.” The journey was a gauntlet of mundane perils. They navigated treacherous plains of broken concrete, forded a stream that smelled faintly of chemicals and regret, and gave a wide berth to a pack of feral, surprisingly well-groomed poodles that now subsisted on anything slower than they were. Finally, the megastore loomed, a cathedral to forgotten consumerism. The automatic doors were, unsurprisingly, manual now, permanently wedged open by the skeleton of a shopping trolley. The interior was a canyon of toppled shelves and the ghostly, faded echoes of brands that no longer meant anything. “Right,” Midas whispered, his voice echoing in the vast silence. “Aisle seven. Canned goods. Look for the cheerful labels with pictures of unnaturally perfect fruit.” They crept forward. The only sound was the scuff of Midas’s boots and the occasional, soft whirr from his backpack. *“Have you had your break today?”* Chewy inquired brightly. “Not yet. Hoping it won’t be my bones,” Midas replied, prying a collapsed shelving unit apart with his club. And then he saw it. A glint of gold and red. A single, dusty can of ‘Sunshine Delight Sliced Peaches in Heavy Syrup’. It was a beacon of hope, a jewel in the dust. It was also, he realized with a sinking feeling, perched precariously on a high ledge, behind a tangled web of what appeared to be the skeletal remains of a promotional display for a children’s cartoon. “Of course it is,” he sighed. “Nothing can ever just be in reach, can it?” He fashioned a makeshift hook from a piece of rebar and began the delicate operation of fishing for the can. He stretched, he strained, the tip of the rebar trembling inches from his prize. *“The ultimate driving machine,”* Chewy stated, with sudden and inappropriate vigour. The unexpected declaration made Midas jump. The rebar clattered against the ledge. The can wobbled. Midas held his breath. It settled back into place. He shot a glare at the koala. “Not helping.” He tried again, this time using the golf club for extra reach. He had it! The hook snagged the ring-pull. He began to gently, ever so gently, pull it towards him. A deep, guttural growl rumbled through the aisle. Midas froze. Slowly, he turned his head. Standing at the end of the aisle was the largest, most ill-tempered-looking raccoon he had ever seen. It was the size of a particularly robust dog, and it regarded Midas not with fear, but with the proprietary annoyance of a landlord discovering a tenant in arrears. This was its peaches. “Ah,” said Midas. The raccoon charged. What followed was a frantic ballet of panic. Midas yanked the can, which flew off the ledge and into his pack, directly beside Chewy. He swung the golf club, not to hit the beast, but to vault over a nearby stack of pallets. The raccoon, undeterted, scrambled after him with terrifying agility, knocking over a tower of bleach bottles that had, miraculously, survived the apocalypse. The cap of one popped off, and a stream of miraculously still-potent bleach shot across the floor. Midas slipped. The raccoon slipped. They both went skidding down the newly-bleached aisle in a chaotic, snarling, flailing mess. They crashed through the remains of the ‘Seasonal Goods’ section, becoming entangled in a network of ancient, brittle Christmas lights and plastic holly. A spark. A fizzle. A sudden, spectacular shower of multicoloured sparks erupted from a tangled cord as the decades-old lights short-circuited. The raccoon, deciding that peaches were no longer worth this level of electrical inconvenience, emitted a final shriek of outrage and fled back into the gloom. Midas lay wheezing on the floor, wrapped in fairy lights, smelling powerfully of chlorine and singed hair. *“You’re in good hands,”* Chewy intoned from the backpack. “I really am not,” Midas coughed. The journey home was a sombre, squelching affair. He was damp, bleached in patches, and mildly electrocuted. But he had the peaches. They arrived back at the ‘Bespoke Artisanal’ ruins as the sun began to bleed out behind the skyline. Midas dumped his pack, pulled out the precious can, and stared at it. His triumph felt hollow, earned at too high a cost to his dignity. He looked at Chewy, who was gazing into the middle distance, a clump of tinsel stuck to his ear. “Well,” Midas said, holding up the can. “We got it. The mission was a success, I suppose.” Chewy’s head rotated a few degrees. There was a soft, internal click. *“Sorry—the fun starts now!”* he chirped. Midas turned the can over. The label on the back was peeling. He picked at it, revealing not gold, not peach, but a dull, greyish metallic surface. He scratched harder. There, stamped into the metal, were the words: **‘CREAMED CORN.’** He sat there for a long time, holding the can of creamed corn, wrapped in tinsel, smelling of bleach. On the wall beside him, his animatronic survival buddy offered his final analysis of the day’s endeavours. *“Think different,”* Chewy said. Midas put his head in his hands. He really, really did.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a competent, genuinely funny Pratchett-adjacent apocalypse story. Its central conceit—Chewy as an animatronic koala spouting corrupted advertising slogans ("Simply un-be-lievably soft," "Reach out and touch someone," "Think different")—is the story's strongest asset, creating reliable comic irony through juxtaposition of cheerful corporate inanity against survival stakes. The running gag is well-paced and escalates cleverly, culminating in the "Sorry—the fun starts now!" beat that pivots into the twist. The plot adheres tightly to the brief: deliberation at base, mission gone sideways (raccoon landlord, bleach slip, electrocution via Christmas lights), return home "worse for wear" in multiple ways. The creamed corn mislabel twist is a satisfying, Pratchett-flavored anticlimax—petty, deflating, and thematically consistent with Midas's name and luck. Strengths: the wry, dry tone is sustained throughout; the prose is economical and controlled; imagery ("a bleary and indifferent eye," "cathedral to forgotten consumerism," the raccoon's "proprietary annoyance of a landlord discovering a tenant in arrears") is vivid without tipping into purple. Dialogue between Midas and Chewy is the story's engine and works well as deadpan call-and-response. Weaknesses: the piece is more pastiche than original—Pratchett's footnote-style digressions and philosophical absurdism are largely absent, replaced by straightforward snark. The feral poodles are introduced and never pay off (Chekhov unfired). Midas is somewhat thin as a character; his "hapless" nature is asserted more than developed. The middle action sequence occasionally rushes ("What followed was a frantic ballet of panic" tells rather than shows, though it partially redeems itself with the bleach-slick detail). Some typos ("undeterted") slightly mar the polish. The emotional range is narrow—wry amusement throughout, with little depth or complexity, though that's arguably appropriate to the brief. The ending's darkness (hollow triumph, creamed corn) is well-earned and tonally congruent. No unearned transformations; no overwrought sentimentality. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 74.8
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell above the door of ‘Penblwydd Hedd’ – ‘Peaceful Birthday’ – chimed a soft, discordant note as the man stumbled in, bringing a gust of damp Welsh air with him. He moved with a strange, hurried grace, like a dancer avoiding rain, and immediately shrank into the shadowy alcove by the travel section, his expensive coat pulled tight. Eluned looked up from re-shelving a stack of vintage Ordnance Survey maps. Her shop was a sanctuary of quiet, of dust motes dancing in the weak afternoon light, and this sudden, furtive energy felt like an intrusion. “Can I help you?” she asked, her voice calm, a product of the hills that cradled the town of Llanelyd. The man offered a smile that was dazzling, practiced, and utterly out of place. It was a smile she’d seen beaming from the side of a double-decker bus in Cardiff. Rhys Vaughan. Film star. Professional charmer. “Just… browsing,” he said, his voice a low, melodic baritone that didn’t match his skittish eyes, which flickered towards the bay window. “Marvellous weather for it.” Eluned followed his glance. Outside, a silver people-carrier with blacked-out windows idled at the curb. “You’re avoiding the weather, then?” His smile tightened at the edges. “Something like that. The forecast called for a deluge of… pests.” He straightened up, the performance beginning. “This is a wonderful place. Truly. A bastion of culture.” “It’s a bookshop,” Eluned said flatly, turning back to her maps. “We sell books.” “And maps!” he said, a little too enthusiastically, gesturing to the stack in her hands. He moved closer, the scent of expensive cologne cutting through the smell of old paper. “I have a thing for maps. Always have. There’s a story in every contour line, don’t you think?” She paused, finally giving him her full attention. His eyes were a startlingly clear blue, and for a heartbeat, the polished veneer slipped, revealing something genuinely curious. Or perhaps he was just that good. “Most people just use them to keep from getting lost on Pen y Fan,” she said. “Ah, but that’s the point! The map isn’t just to avoid being lost. It’s to invite discovery.” He leaned against the oak desk, oozing a casual intimacy he hadn’t earned. “For instance, this one,” he said, plucking the top map from her stack without asking. “This region here. That’s not just a valley. That’s a story of glacial retreat, of ancient sheep trails. You can see the history in the lines.” Eluned raised an eyebrow. It was a decent line, well-delivered. Probably worked in every cocktail bar from Soho to Malibu. “You know your ordnance surveys.” “A hobby,” he said, waving a dismissive hand, though he clearly preened at the faint praise. “I like to know the lay of the land. In all things.” He gave her a look that was meant to be smouldering. She found it vaguely amusing, like a cat trying to be a lion. “It’s a good hobby. Grounding.” She took the map back from him, her fingers brushing his. She ignored the little jolt that went up her arm. “Better than whatever it is you usually do. Setting off car alarms, from what I read.” Rhys Vaughan laughed, a rich, surprised sound that seemed more genuine than anything else he’d done. “You’ve read about me?” “I read the headlines while queueing at the co-op. It’s unavoidable. ‘Rhys Vaughan’s Latest Blow-Up’ is usually next to ‘Half-Price Welsh Cakes’.” He looked genuinely put-out for a second, his ego visibly prickling. He was a man who expected to be the main event, not the B-side to a baked good. “They print such nonsense.” “I’m sure.” Her tone was dry as the dust on the top shelves. She started sorting the maps again, a clear dismissal. He should have left then. His charm had failed, his celebrity was irrelevant here. But her indifference was a novelty, a puzzle. He didn’t move. “They are nonsense,” he insisted, a petulant edge creeping into his voice. “Last week they said I threw a tantrum over the temperature of my espresso. I don’t even drink espresso. I prefer tea. Proper tea. Builders’. Two sugars.” Eluned couldn’t help a small smile. “A man of the people.” “See? You mock me.” He sighed, a performance of world-weariness. “Everyone does.” “I don’t think everyone does, Mr. Vaughan. I think quite a lot of people like you very much. That’s rather the point of your job, isn’t it?” He was silent for a moment, watching her competent hands smooth the creases from a map of the Brecon Beacons. The performance was faltering, leaving something more vulnerable in its wake. “It’s exhausting,” he said, and for the first time, it sounded true. Eluned glanced at him. The famous bravado was gone. He just looked like a man, hiding in a bookshop. She felt her carefully maintained defences soften, just a fraction. “This right here,” she said, pointing to a spot on the map she was holding, changing the subject. “That’s not an official path. It’s a farmer’s track. Leads to a waterfall that isn’t on any tourist brochure. The OS map hints at it, but you have to want to find it.” His attention snapped to the map, all artifice gone. “Really? How do you know?” “Because,” she said, a hint of pride in her voice, “I’ve walked it. I’ve walked most of them. The maps are a starting point. The land tells you the real story.” He looked from the intricate lines on the paper to her face, and a slow, real smile spread across his. It transformed him, making him younger, less polished, infinitely more attractive. “You’re a cartographer-explorer,” he said, and the flattery felt different this time. Specific. Earnest. “I’m a bookseller who likes a quiet walk,” she corrected, but she could feel a blush warming her cheeks. She was flustered, and she hated that he could probably see it. He saw it. His eyes lingered on her face, and the rogue’s charm returned, but it was quieter now, tempered with something like respect. “I’d love to hear about that walk sometime. I’m… staying locally. For a bit. Hiding from the pests.” The bell on the door chimed again. The people-carrier outside revved its engine and pulled away. The moment broke. “Looks like the forecast has cleared,” Eluned said, her voice steadier than she felt. Rhys Vaughan straightened his coat, the famous persona settling back over him like a familiar cloak, but his eyes held hers for a beat too long. “It has. Thank you. For the… shelter.” He started for the door, then paused, turning back. “The offer stands. About the walk. I’ll bring the tea. Builders’. Two sugars.” Before she could form a rebuttal, he was gone, the bell echoing behind him. Eluned stood alone in the sudden quiet of the shop, her heart beating a rhythm that felt entirely new. She looked down at the map in her hands, her finger still resting on the secret path to the waterfall. For the first time in a long time, she felt a little lost. And, despite herself, strangely discovered.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The scene fulfills the brief competently: a famous actor (Rhys Vaughan) ducks into a Welsh bookshop to escape paparazzi, meets the owner (Eluned), and their dialogue carries the requested dynamic — his charm offensive fails against her dry immunity, which provokes genuine interest in him and flusters her inwardly. The Welsh setting is present but somewhat decorative (Llanelyd, Pen y Fan, Ordnance Survey maps, co-op queue, Welsh cakes) — the maps motif is actually the scene's cleverest device, giving the conversation a concrete object and metaphor (the secret path to the waterfall mirroring the discovery of the person). Dialogue is the strength. The voices are distinct: Rhys's performative baritone with its preening and petulance ("I don't even drink espresso. I prefer tea. Proper tea. Builders'. Two sugars."), and Eluned's dry, grounded wit ("'Rhys Vaughan's Latest Blow-Up' is usually next to 'Half-Price Welsh Cakes'"). The ego-prickle moment — "a man who expected to be the main event, not the B-side to a baked good" — is a sharp, funny beat that shows the fragile ego well. The "cartographer-explorer" exchange lands the shift from performed flattery to earnest, specific attention, which is the emotional pivot the prompt requested. Weaknesses: the narration occasionally tells rather than shows ("He was a man who expected to be the main event", "She felt her carefully maintained defences soften", "She was flustered, and she hated that he could probably see it"). Some lines are stock romance fare: "a jolt that went up her arm", "his eyes held hers for a beat too long", "her heart beating a rhythm that felt entirely new". The ending is a touch neat and over-sweet ("strangely discovered" is a strained final flourish), and the transformation of Rhys from rogue to vulnerable is somewhat quick, though the prompt itself mandates that arc, so it's partially earned by design. The shop name "Penblwydd Hedd" translated as "Peaceful Birthday" is an odd, unexplained choice (Hedd = peace, penblwydd = birthday — a strange name for a bookshop) that reads as a Welsh-flavored detail without real grounding. Prose is clean and controlled, with a few genuinely good images ("like a dancer avoiding rain", "like a cat trying to be a lion"). Pacing is tight; no meandering. Emotionally it engages without ever surprising. It's a polished, professional genre scene — charming, but operating well within romance conventions. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 72.5
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The silence was a tomb. After the frantic scramble through the chaos of the guild’s upper warrens—the shouts of confused enforcers, the clatter of dropped loot, the panicked scurrying of rats who sensed the sinking of their ship—the hush that enveloped the antechamber of the underhold was profoundly wrong. It was a velvet shroud, thick and suffocating, muffling even the frantic thrum of Aya’s own heart. The air, usually thick with the reek of whale oil, cheap gin, and unwashed bodies, was here cold and still, smelling only of damp stone and a faint, coppery tang. Aya’s gloved hand, poised over the massive, gear-studded iron door, hesitated. Her companions felt it too. Katra, a wisp of a girl with fingers light enough to pluck a coin from a noble’s purse without disturbing the lice in his wig, shifted her weight, her knives silent in their sheaths. Simeon, solid and reliable as the steam-engine he once tended, adjusted his waistcoat. From its pocket came the loud, metronomic *tick… tick… tick…* of his brass chronometer, a sound that now seemed less a measure of time and more a countdown to calamity. “It’s too quiet,” Katra whispered, her voice a breath of steam in the cold air. “The lock’s already been disengaged,” Simeon murmured, his engineer’s eye noting the precise, clean scratches around the mechanism. “Recently. The tumblers are set.” Aya’s blood ran colder than the stone walls. There was no choice but forward. Leveraging her shoulder against the cold iron, she pushed. The door swung inward without a sound, its hinges oiled to a sinister perfection. The underhold was not the dark, forgotten vault she had imagined. Gas-jets hissed within ornate brass sconces, casting a jaundiced, flickering light over a scene of ordered menace. The fabled Scythan artifact—a twisted helix of obsidian and tarnished silver that seemed to drink the light around it—sat undisturbed on a velvet cushion at the room’s centre. But it was not alone. Seated in a high-backed chair of nailed leather and ironwood, as if holding court in her own parlour, was Mistress Anya Kozlov, the Guild Queen herself. She was not languishing in a dank cell in the Iron Gaol. She was here, impeccably dressed in a severe gown of charcoal grey wool, her fingers steepled. Two hulking brutes, their faces scarred and minds hollowed out by cheap narcotics and cheaper violence, flanked her. Their knuckles were wrapped in oil-stained leather, and the gleam of piston-driven knuckle-dusters adorned their fists. They were the Guild’s pure product: brutal, efficient, and utterly devoid of imagination. Aya’s breath caught in her throat. *A trap. It was all a trap. The raid, the arrest… it was a gambit to flush out the ambitious.* “The little mice finally come to nibble the cheese,” Kozlov’s voice was like gravel grinding under a bootheel, smooth yet utterly abrasive. Her eyes, chips of flint in a face of sharp angles and calculated cruelty, swept over them. “And they brought a clockwork man to tell them the time. How… predictable.” Before any of them could move, the brutes were upon them. There was a brief, brutal scuffle—a gasp from Katra, a grunt of pain from Simeon as a piston-enhanced fist drove into his gut. Aya reached for the immateria, for the chilling whispers that coiled in the back of her skull, but a backhanded blow from one of the guards sent her sprawling, her mask knocked askew. The world swam, and when her vision cleared, she was on her knees, her arms pinned behind her back. Katra and Simeon were similarly restrained, the loud *tick… tick… tick…* of the pocket watch now a frantic, captive heartbeat. Kozlov rose and glided forward, her movements unnervingly fluid. With a contemptuous flick of her wrist, she tore the silk mask from Aya’s face. A moment of stunned silence was broken only by the ticking clock. Kozlov’s eyebrows arched, a slow, venomous smile spreading across her thin lips. “Well, well. The whispers were true. The little songbird singing my secrets back to her gilded cage is none other than Lady Aya von Hapsenburg.” She leaned down, her breath smelling of mint and arsenic. “Dabbling in the low arts, my dear? Your mother’s unfortunate… proclivities… were bad enough. But this? This is a far more potent scandal.” Aya’s mind raced, careening through a vortex of terror and shame. Her father’s stern disappointment, the sneers of the court, the inevitable, crushing weight of her family’s ruin. They wouldn’t hang her. No, her station would grant her that small mercy. They would lock her away in some sanitarium, a silent, shamed secret until the end of her days. “You seem to be labouring under a misapprehension, Kozlov,” Aya said, her voice straining to maintain the cool, aristocratic cadence she’d been bred for, even as her knees ached against the cold stone. “My value to you is not as a guild member to be punished. It is as a noblewoman to be ransomed.” Kozlov let out a dry, humourless laugh. “You think I need your family’ money, little girl? I *own* half the magistrates in this district. Coin is a currency of the mundane.” “Coin is not the currency I am offering,” Aya countered, her heart hammering against her ribs. “I am offering *influence*. *Protection*. My disappearance will cause an uproar that not even your owned magistrates can contain. The City Watch will tear this district apart stone by stone. But my safe return… that can be arranged with a single, discreet letter. A tale of a thrilling, albeit foolish, carriage ride gone astray. My father would be eternally… grateful.” She was bargaining with a snake, using the very identity she loathed as her only shield. The irony was a bitter pill. “Gratitude,” Kozlov mused, circling her like a shark smelling blood. “A fleeting commodity. Whereas the spectacle of your unmasking… the humiliation of a great house… that has a lasting value. It reminds every other high-born fool that the gutter is a dangerous place to play.” She stopped, her flinty eyes glinting. “And it deals a far more poetic justice to the daughter of a witch. The apple, it seems, did not fall far from the blighted tree.” *Tick. Tick. Tick.* Simeon struggled against his captor. “Don’t you listen to her, you rust-brained—“ A sharp crack cut him off as a guard silenced him with a blow to the head. Kozlov ignored him, her attention fixed solely on Aya. “You possess her gift, don’t you? The true reason for your rapid ascent. You don’t just play with locks and shadows. You whisper to the things that rustle in the corners of the world.” Aya said nothing, her silence a confirmation. A dark, avaricious light ignited in Kozlov’s eyes. “The artifact,” she said, gesturing to the obsidian helix. “It has never responded to any of my… associates. Its secrets remain locked. But perhaps it requires a key of a different metal. A darker temper.” She straightened up, her decision made. “The boy and the urchin are of no consequence. Take them to the rendering vats.” Katra whimpered, and Simeon’s ticking watch seemed to falter for a terrible second. “Wait!” Aya’s voice cracked, the aristocratic veneer finally splintering. “You need me compliant. You need me willing. Harm them, and you will get nothing from me but silence. I will throw myself from the highest window of my father’s manor before I aid you.” Kozlov studied her, the gaslight carving deep shadows into her face, giving her the look of a gothic gargoyle come to life. The silence stretched, filled only by the relentless, metallic ticking, marking the seconds of a life that was no longer her own. “Very well,” the Guild Queen said finally, her voice a soft, sinister promise. “They will live. For now. Let us adjourn to my quarters, Lady von Hapsenburg. We have so very much to discuss about your… inheritance.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response is a competent, professional-grade scene that hits nearly all the requested beats: the trio enters the underhold, confronts the un-incarcerated guild leader, is captured, Aya is unmasked, and she negotiates her value as a hostage while internally grappling with the consequences of exposure. The prose is polished, atmospheric, and consistent with the gritty Victorian/gothic brief — gas-jets, brass chronometers, whale oil, arsenic on the breath. The ticking watch as a recurring motif is a nice touch, though it edges toward being overused as a dramatic device. Strengths: The scene is coherent and well-paced; the trap reveal is handled economically; Kozlov is given a distinct, menacing voice ("Coin is a currency of the mundane"); Aya's internal monologue about sanitariums versus hanging effectively conveys her class-based calculus; the negotiation has genuine back-and-forth tension, and Kozlov's counter-arguments (spectacle as currency, gratitude as fleeting) are genuinely smart villain logic rather than strawman posturing. The ending — sparing the companions to secure Aya's compliance, then pivoting to the artifact — is a satisfying escalation rather than a cop-out. Weaknesses: The piece leans on stock phrasings — "voice was like gravel grinding under a bootheel," "circling her like a shark," "a slow, venomous smile," "flinty eyes" — which are serviceable but clichéd. Some similes are stacked two or three to a sentence, tipping into overwrought territory ("a velvet shroud, thick and suffocating, muffling even the frantic thrum"). The capture itself is glossed over quickly (appropriate, since a fight scene was forbidden, but the "brief, brutal scuffle" is told rather than shown). Katra and Simeon are thin — Katra gets one whisper and a whimper; Simeon exists mostly as his watch. The "brutes" are pure archetype. Aya's aristocratic mask cracking at "Wait!" is a good beat, but her emotional register stays fairly level throughout; the terror is narrated more than felt. The prose occasionally over-explains its own irony ("The irony was a bitter pill"). The reveal that the raid was a gambit to flush out the ambitious is delivered as Aya's inference in a single line — a clever idea given only cursory treatment. Overall this is solid, engaging genre fiction that fulfills the brief with craft, held back from excellence by familiar imagery, underdeveloped secondary characters, and a tendency toward ornamental rather than essential description.
